newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FOCUS - Ukraine hryvnia closes week on record-high.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Ukraine hryvnia closes week on record-high.

text.p: Ukraine's hryvnia currency rounded off a buoyant week by bouncing up to a near record 1.765 to the dollar on Friday, leaving economists and bankers watching to see whether the authorities would push it up further.

"Theoretically, yes, they could appreciate the currency," said one Western economist, who asked not to be named. "The IMF (International Monetary Fund) was in favour of currency appreciation because of the huge flows of financing to Ukraine."
The hryvnia, introduced at 1.76 last September to replace the interim karbovanets currency, stood at 1.85 to the dollar on Monday on the Ukraine Interbank Currency Exchange.

Another Western economic expert said the rise was due to inflows of some $3.2 billion in balance of payments support promised by foreign institutions and donor nations, combined with increased hryvnia buying by foreigners getting into the lucrative Treasury-bill market.
"The $3.2 billion represents eight percent of GDP (gross domestic product), and this creates a very high re-evaluation of the currency," he said.
"And there is madness about the T-bill market," he added.

Central bank chief Viktor Yushchenko, recently re-appointed by parliament to a four-year term, has said implementation of a currency corridor or trading band was a theoretical issue until parliament passed the budget in March or April.

But the expert said a corridor was already in place, since the central bank -- with hard currency reserves estimated at about $3 billion -- intervened regularly on the exchange to maintain the hryvnia at a specific level.
"They would never announce this formally," he said.

Central bank officials have said bank policy is directed at stopping the hryvnia from rising or falling more than 10 percent over a year. The lowest rate in 1996 was 191,100 karbovanets (1.911 hryvnia) and the highest was 1.760 against the dollar.

International donors pledged last December to give Ukraine about $3.5 billion in assistance this year alone, and the country is also expecting a $2.5-$3.0 billion, three-year credit from the IMF which is conditional on the final budget.

The economist said increased foreign investment in T-bills, whose yields fell to about 30 percent for three- and six-month discount paper and around 37 percent for nine- and 12-month securities on Thursday, boded well for investments this year.
Ukraine has also forecast annual inflation will slow to 25 percent from 39.7 in 1996, although zero growth is predicted.

But Ukrainian bankers expected the government would regulate foreign participation on the T-bill market soon, even though a law proposed by the Finance Ministry was quietly shelved this week after it was rejected by the Justice Ministry.
"The central bank is having big problems regulating the rate and growth is having a big impact on exporters," said Volodymyr Yatsenko, head of the currency department at Privatbank in Dnipropetrovsk.

Yatsenko said the central bank could devalue the hryvnia to scare off investors. "The rate was almost at 1.89 before it started to rise, and many think that it will end about 1.95 this year. So the real yield will be lower in dollars and will attract foreigners less strongly."
